Sorry to interrupt your Saturday routine. I know my team and I email you a lot. But I couldn't let another moment pass without reaching out to say _thank you._
Your support is what's made our recent surge in momentum possible. Your generosity has helped bring this race to a tie, and I couldn't be more grateful. I hope when you see poll after poll showing us within striking distance of Greg Abbott, you feel proud of what your support has helped accomplish.
**[With just THREE days left until Election Day, I'm coming specifically to our most engaged supporters with a special request: I'm going to ask if you'll increase your support by donating $10, $5, or even $3 today. We are so close to the finish line, but I need your continued support to help get me through this final stretch. ](https://substack.com/redirect/c569c3e0-30d6-4d0c-9f83-56402b83a061?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
_This race is ours to win._
But according to the numbers our Finance Team just pulled, we're running out of resources at the worst possible time. There's just three days left before final ballots will be cast, and we're leaving it all on the table. **[That's why I'm humbly asking you to please chip in whatever you can today while there's still enough time to make an impact.](https://substack.com/redirect/c569c3e0-30d6-4d0c-9f83-56402b83a061?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
Grassroots supporters like you are the force behind this campaign. Working people on this team coming together and chipping in small amounts at a time have put Greg Abbott and his corporate billionaire donors on defense. That is no small feat.
Thank you, thank you, thank you. It is because of you that we will flip Texas.
-- Gina

But while the number of Americans still held by Russia is widely reported to be [eight or nine](https://substack.com/redirect/f64284cb-cf5b-4137-bef3-5175cfd62045?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), Loomer Unleashed has exclusively learned that the number is actually much higher: 22.
Earlier this week, Laura Loomer spoke with an official at the center of the negotiations to get the rest of the American hostages released. During the Iran Hostage Crisis almost 50 years ago, the Islamic regime held [66 Americans hostage](https://substack.com/redirect/72341b86-8e02-4b87-9512-9bfc4e27492c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). That's three times as many of our citizens as Russia has in prison today, but it seemed like there was 1,000 times more attention paid to Iran at the time.

And there's no reason to not get tougher with Russia, according to retired Lt. Gen. Ben Hodges, who has long warned that "[Russia is already at war with the West](https://substack.com/redirect/12989e4d-7172-4df6-b1d6-a36e88e949ba?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)." At a recent conference, Hodges said Russia's position is far weaker than it [appears.](https://substack.com/redirect/6aef04eb-a99b-4a04-b6fd-b60dafeb861e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
"Russia is a superpower only in the heads of European and American elites. It cannot defeat Ukraine. Why is Europe always so terrified of Russia? Why is the U.S. so terrified about 'provoking' Russia? We should act with so much more self-confidence."
Likely frustrated that he has been so unsuccessful in Ukraine, Putin has stepped up his attacks this month. As we reported earlier this week, the Russian army conducted massive attacks on a [thermal power station](https://substack.com/redirect/87e3b01a-6616-4fd0-90b9-dabcd7e0b162?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and [several other facilities](https://substack.com/redirect/c97d4f15-41e4-4750-9ce0-a1826c4608c1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) owned by DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company. This has brought temporary disruptions to Ukrainian power infrastructure. If Putin continues on this course, it seems like his goal is to leave millions of Ukrainians without power right as they head into their frigid winter season.
When Loomer visited Ukraine personally in July, she was able to tour DTEK facilities and interview DTEK employees in Kyiv while Russians were actively firing drones and missiles at the facility. This week, a 41-year-old DTEK miner was [killed by a Russian drone strike on Pavlohrad](https://substack.com/redirect/96605f64-9cec-43d0-b1e1-d3632964551c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). A separate missile strike on Kyiv this week killed another Ukrainian, and even a [dog](https://substack.com/redirect/db6ab9e9-89c4-4845-b61a-2bb4a86f7605?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).

Friend,

If you only read one email from me this month, please make it this one.

As a pastor, I learned something early: _you can’t ask people to show up after the doors have closed._

Right now, the doors are about to close on our **LAST End-of-Month deadline** before the Midterm elections on November 3rd.

After that, there are no more reports. No more chances to catch up. _**Just Election Day, and whatever we have in hand.**_

And what we have in hand will decide whether North Carolina has the resources to hold the line, and whether Republicans keep the Majority.

We're just days away from Election Day, and the pressure is on. But not for the reasons you might think...
The truth is: I don’t want to let you down.
You are the heart of this campaign. Since the very beginning, grassroots donors have made it possible to compete with massive spending from special interests. You’ve proven that when working people come together, we can win:

I hope I didn’t interrupt your trick-or-treating, but this can’t wait:
Election Day is just three days away, and I wanted to take the opportunity to thank each and every one of our dedicated grassroots supporters.
Without folks like you, we wouldn’t be in a strong position to defend IL-17, and I truly appreciate your steadfast support.
But we can’t take anything for granted. This race will be razor-close, and it could determine control of the House for the next two years.
There’s nothing spookier than that!

body:
Early numbers are in...
|
Friend,
I'll be honest with you... I'm not great at asking for money. It's the part of this job I hate the most.
I didn't spend my twenties learning how to fundraise to run for office. I spent them flying H-46 helicopters for the Navy and deploying to the Persian Gulf.
And when I came home, I didn't become a lobbyist who took clients out to expensive dinners. I used my GI Bill to become a Geriatric Nurse Practitioner. My "networking" was holding the hands of our seniors and listening to their stories, not cutting backroom deals.
That's really who I am...a Helicopter Pilot...a Nurse Practitioner... and a Mom trying to raise four happy and healthy kids in a world that feels like it's going in the wrong direction most days.
[I didn't run for Congress for the title. I ran because I looked at the country my children were inheriting, and I felt sick to my stomach. clean_body: Early numbers are in... | Friend, I'll be honest with you... I'm not great at asking for money. It's the part of this job I hate the most. I didn't spend my twenties learning how to fundraise to run for office. I spent them flying H-46 helicopters for the Navy and deploying to the Persian Gulf. And when I came home, I didn't become a lobbyist who took clients out to expensive dinners. I used my GI Bill to become a Geriatric Nurse Practitioner. My "networking" was holding the hands of our seniors and listening to their stories, not cutting backroom deals. That's really who I am...a Helicopter Pilot...a Nurse Practitioner... and a Mom trying to raise four happy and healthy kids in a world that feels like it's going in the wrong direction most days. But here is the hard truth: fighting the radical Left and standing up for our values is incredibly expensive. I don't have a massive machine behind me. I don't have someone who can write blank checks on a whim. I know things are tight right now. I see it at the grocery store just like you do. Get Involved

SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 2026

HI EVERYONE,

Happy Halloween! Nothing is scarier than another four years of failed Democrat leadership in our state, but you can help stop it.
Election Day is just three days away, and we need everyone in this final push: making calls, texting friends, and getting out the
vote.

Phone calls are the single biggest way you can make an impact on this race. There are still Republicans who haven't turned in
their ballots, and they need to hear that there's still time to vote in person and help save our state.

You can call from anywhere you have cell service or Wi-Fi:

1. Download the Right Insight app and log in with your email.

2. Join one of our call projects.

3. Tap "Start Questionnaire" to pull up the script, and start dialing!

JOIN US AT OUR FINAL EVENTS

We have two big events coming up, and we'd love to see you at one or both! Come show our candidates your support, and bring your
friends, family, and neighbors who want to meet them before Election Day.

Help us fill the room

You can also help with turnout right from Right Insight. Tap "LinkUp" at the bottom right of your screen, sync your contacts, and
invite your friends, family, and neighbors to these events in just a few taps.

body:

| [](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1787&source=&t=1&akid=5173%2E124072%2EDPIaLn) | | | |

Peter,
I normally wouldn’t be so blunt, but I’m just going to come right out and say it: **I need you to chip in $5 to my campaign for U.S. Senate right now.**
Senate control is at stake here in North Carolina. The GOP has poured tens of millions into false attack ads against me, and President Trump has personally come to NC three times to smear my name. With three days left in this race, their lies have reached millions of North Carolinians on the airwaves and online – and unless we have the grassroots resources to fight back, my MAGA opponent might beat us across the finish line.
**The only way we can stay on track to win is by hitting our final $5 million end-of-month goal tonight.**
Tomorrow – let alone three days from now – will be too late, so please use this link to rush $5 or any amount before midnight: [**_https:/ /secure.actblue.com/contribute/page/cvf-email-26_**](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1787&amount=5&t=8&akid=5173%2E124072%2EDPIaLn)
Thanks so much,
Roy Cooper

body:
| Before you don the makeup and costumes with your loved ones or press play on your favorite scary movie, I have one last request.
---
[](https://act.adamschiff.com/go/8022?amount=10&t=1&refcode=aschiff_email_103126_halloweenthrowback&akid=10918%2E5257348%2EciZqP7)
Derek, I thought I’d dig up an old photo of me holding my son on his very first Halloween. [](https://act.adamschiff.com/go/8046?t=10&amount=10&refcode=aschiff_email_103126_halloweenthrowback&akid=10918%2E5257348%2EciZqP7) Amid all the tumult of this campaign season, with Donald Trump threatening lawsuits to invalidate votes before they’ve even been tallied and the world’s first trillionaire, Elon Musk, doling out hundreds of millions of dollars for MAGA candidates, it’s easy to lose sight of why we do this work in the first place. _I do it for my family and for yours, Derek._ Because we deserve a government that’s accountable to the people. Graduating from West Point was just the beginning of my eight years in the United States Army.
During Operation Iraqi Freedom, I led Apache Helicopter Platoons, and I feel like I spent more time in the air than I did on the ground. Some nights, I didn’t know if I’d make it through the next day, and every mission I flew, I went into the unknown. **Throughout my service, I had the honor of receiving a Combat Action Badge and two Air Medals. **
**I wouldn’t trade my time in the service for anything, but I’ll be honest, it was good coming home, and _I can rest easy knowing I did my country proud._**

clean_body: If we turn out every Democratic voter in Wisconsin, we’re going to win in a landslide. | | | | Hey, Derek, it’s Ben Wikler, former WisDems chair. We have 3 days left. And the fight we’ve all been fighting—sixteen years of organizing to win a Democratic governorship and state legislature in Wisconsin—is on a knife’s edge. The election-denying billionaires on the right know the stakes in this election. That’s why they’ve poured $34 million into helping Tom Tiffany. But there’s one thing they didn’t count on. You. You’ve powered Democratic victories year over year in the hardest-fought state in the country. You beat Scott Walker, you flipped the state Supreme Court majority, you ended gerrymandered maps. And in these final days, the power is in your hands to ensure that David Crowley and the Dems win it all. If we turn out every Democratic voter in Wisconsin, we’re going to win in a landslide. We’ve seen this movie before: Elon Musk tried to buy the state Supreme Court race in 2025. We threw him out of the state and elected Susan Crawford by ten percentage points. Now, Elon Musk is back—and along with him, three more MAGA mega-billionaires who are flooding the airwaves with ads and flying canvassers in from Texas to knock on Wisconsinites’ doors. But you know our secret weapon: people power. Our organizers are working with teams of volunteers in every corner of the state, right now, to talk to their neighbors, make phone calls, and build a blue wave from the bottom up. I was proud to support that grassroots operation when I was chair. Devin Remiker and the whole WisDems team are doing an amazing job now to organize their way to even higher heights. The GOP has more money, but at the grassroots level, they’re not even close to what you’ve helped build. Now we have to run through the tape. Your money pays for (expensive!) gas mileage as organizers drive from canvass launch to canvass launch, for clipboards for volunteers, and for printing costs for door hangers. Good evening, Peter. Tonight is a big night for my campaign. Tomorrow is our last day of early voting. There are still huge chunks of undecided voters out there, and we have serious outreach to them planned for tomorrow. We’re gearing up for a historic final sprint to the finish line, but that means we have some seriously ambitious fundraising goals we still need to hit. But forget about that for a moment. I want to talk about why I’m in this race to begin with. I was a junior in high school on 9/11 when the Twin Towers fell. The next day, I began my West Point application. After graduating, I did six overseas deployments serving in combat zones like Iraq and Afghanistan. I did that out of a love for this country. Back then, I never thought that the greatest threat to America’s future would come from within our own borders. But the people running this administration do not share our values – or the values of the generations of Americans who fought and sacrificed to make this country better. **So I made the decision to run for Congress, again, out of love for this country.** My opponent, Mike Lawler, has become a rubber stamp for Trump and the MAGA agenda. body:

The American people are fired up, and they’re ready to fight back at the ballot box. **But right now, we’re pacing to fall short of our $2 million end-of-month fundraising goal.** And that’s not some arbitrary number, Derek. Our team carefully sets these goals to make sure that we can continue to expand our midterm operations ahead of Election Day — knocking doors, making calls, and turning out Democratic voters in key battlegrounds. **Hitting this goal in 6 hours could be the difference between reaching enough voters to see Democratic wins across the country or not.** [**So, we’re respectfully asking you to chip in $7 to the DNC before midnight tonight to help us get back on track. Friend, I wanted you to see this incredible news: **The Cook Political Report and Nate Silver announced our race is a _Toss Up,_ meaning it is among the most competitive across the whole country.**
This came after a New York Times/Siena poll showed me tied with Roger Marshall.
All these dead heat polls and updated ratings tell me two things:
**1.** We can win this race.

subject: One final goal before November 3
body:
Hi friend,
We are finally here. On Tuesday, all of the work we’ve put in, the conversations we’ve had, the doors we’ve knocked, and the communities we’ve brought together will come down to one thing: making our voices heard at the ballot box.
I am deeply grateful for the opportunity to serve our community. Every day of this campaign has been dedicated to building real representation in Washington – representation focused on passing meaningful legislation that improves people's lives.
We've put in the work to ensure our district has a strong, effective voice in Congress, and I couldn't be prouder of what we've built together.
With Election Day just days away, I'm thinking about the work ahead, both for our community here in CA-30 and for the next Congress. From lowering housing and healthcare costs to protecting our fundamental rights, there is so much more we need to accomplish.
As we prepare for the next chapter, I'm grateful for every supporter who has helped make this work possible.
And I hope you know that anything you can give will help keep our momentum going strong in the final days and hours. We’ll never take anything for granted. If you can, please pitch in before midnight.

Here’s what I need you to hear: 2.7 points is not a lost race. This is one of the most competitive governor’s races in the country, and it will be decided by turnout, by organizing, and by what we do in these final days.

subject: So goes Ohio, so goes the Senate
disclaimer_text: Paid for by the Ohio Democratic Party and not authorized by any candidate or candidate's committee
body:
We have two options.
|
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/142639394/657557760/407551833?refcode=ODP_ATA_EM_FR_BrownSplit_261031_T3_1&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMjEvMS84OTI0NyIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI3N2FjZTQ2MS04MGQ1LWYxMTEtYmY1Yi0wMDBkM2E1NDQ0MmUiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=t03SsnNK036xxwvz0J2EWCxm13XotYADIJaxrqapqT0=)
Hey there,

Everyone from election analysts to political pundits has been saying that this race in Ohio could, and very likely will, decide which party controls the U.S. Senate.

**Now, Republican strategists are even admitting it too.** One strategist aligned with Trump recently told Politico:

_“Ohio is going to be your bellwether of what kind of night it is ... I think – I do truly think – as Ohio goes, the Senate goes right now.”_

This race will set the stage, and we have two options before us: We can join together, flip Ohio’s must-win seat, and take back the Senate. Or, we can take our foot off the gas in this final sprint, let Husted win, and cede control of the Senate to the GOP until 2029 at least.

Volunteers and staffers will be calling, texting, and knocking doors right to the end because believe it or not, there are people who will wait until the last moment to decide whether to jump in their car and run down to the polling station.
We’re going to fight to the end for those people and everyone in TX-03, because they deserve nothing less than us giving our all.
Almost there, let’s do this together!
Very respectfully,
Evan Hunt Democratic Nominee TX-03

subject: My last-ditch request
body:
Peter — it’s
James, and I’m reaching out with a last-ditch request.

Our October fundraising deadline is at midnight tonight. I just checked
our ActBlue, and we’re pacing behind where we need to be to reach our
budget goal. So I’m asking:

Can I count on you to make your first ActBlue donation of just $1 so we
can flip Texas’ Senate seat? Here’s your personal donation link:

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261031-3-ak&t=1001&akid=1182%2E1347274%2ElG82x3 ]https://secure.actblue.com/donate/jt-em-2026q4?email=dpwillis67@gmail.com

There’s a reason why billionaire mega-donors are spending $200 million
against our movement. It’s because they know we are on the verge of a
political earthquake.

Texans turned out in record numbers for early voting because they are
ready for change. They are fired up for a political system that fights for
working people, not just for those at the very top.

But we can’t take our eye off the ball yet. We’ve come too far to come up
short now.

This race could be decided by just a few thousand votes, so we need all
hands on deck to share our message and make sure every Talafreako gets to
the polls.

We have to make our last spending decisions after tonight’s deadline, and
we’re still short of where our budget projections showed we needed to be.

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261031-3-ak&t=1002&akid=1182%2E1347274%2ElG82x3 ]Please donate to help us reach our goals before our October fundraising
deadline. These numbers are not arbitrary. We’ve calculated exactly what
we need to raise in order to win.

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261031-3-ak&t=1005&akid=1182%2E1347274%2ElG82x3 ]CONTRIBUTE

Thank you,

James Talarico

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261031-3-ak&t=1006&akid=1182%2E1347274%2ElG82x3 ]'New York Times: In Texas, Talarico Inspires a Recurring Blue-Tinted
Dream In the go-big-or-go-home collective consciousness of Texas, no
ambition is deemed too reckless, no daydream too wild. Save perhaps one.
It is the idea, fantastical to many as it is irresistible to others, that
the Democrats will win a statewide race in Texas for the first time in 32
years. According to the latest New York Times/Siena University poll of the
race for U.S. Senate, James Talarico, a 37-year-old state legislator seen
by national Democrats as one of the breakout stars of this cycle, is ahead
of his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, the state’s scandal-plagued attorney
general, by six points. The poll was conducted from Sept. 21 to Sept. 30.
A survey from mid-September, the ReconMR/Siena Research Institute poll,
also showed the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Gina Hinojosa, four
points ahead of the three-term G.O.P. incumbent, Greg Abbott, the most
dominant political figure in Texas. Cue the fluttering heartbeats. Cue, as
well, the eye-rolls. Given how thoroughly Republicans have dominated the
state, and how the hopes of Democrats have repeatedly crashed, some Texas
pollsters remain skeptical. “At some point, you do get conditioned by all
that’s happened in the past,” said James Henson, the director of the
University of Texas at Austin’s Texas Politics Project. “I mean, you look
at the trends and you have to admit that something’s going on. But you
still don’t want to believe your lying eyes, because you’ve been burned
for so long.” Mr. Henson was referring to the perennial spectacle of
much-ballyhooed Texas Democratic aspirants face-planting against the Lone
Star State’s red wall. First came Tony Sanchez Jr., the swaggering and
self-funding Laredo oilman whom Gov. Rick Perry dispatched in 2002 by an
18-point margin. Next was the state senator Wendy Davis, who attracted
worldwide attention for her filibuster in the Texas Legislature against an
anti-abortion measure but whom Mr. Abbott demolished by 20 points in 2014.
Finally, the El Paso congressman Beto O’Rourke came up 2.6 points short of
defeating Senator Ted Cruz in 2018 but then suffered a 10-point loss to
Mr. Abbott four years later. Even with the awareness of such humiliations,
Democrats find themselves maintaining that 2026 could, at long last, be
the year. President Trump’s deep unpopularity and the prospect of a blue
wave could, they insist, extend into the state he won by nearly 14 points
in 2024. According to a September survey conducted by Texas Southern
University, Mr. Trump is seven points underwater in Texas. Mr. Talarico
has run an energetic and well-financed campaign, while Mr. Paxton has
staged far fewer public events and has had to rely on outside groups to
fund an attack-ad blitzkrieg against his Democratic opponent. Mr. Abbott,
meanwhile, has outspent Ms. Hinojosa by a 10-to-one ratio, yet has been
unable to build an insurmountable lead. “People have vastly underestimated
Gina,” said Ms. Davis, now a political consultant and a senior adviser to
Planned Parenthood Texas Votes, an advocacy organization. “Dollar for
dollar, she’s running the best statewide campaign we’ve ever seen.” Such
optimism stands in defiance of the political axiom that Texas is where
idealistic Democrats go to be mugged by reality. The party’s demise there
is not a product of ill fortune, Mr. Henson said. “Governor Abbott has
built an impressive election machine that has benefited state-level
Republicans again and again for a decade and a half,” he said. “And the
Democratic machinery here is almost nonexistent.” A ‘Hollowing-Out’ I have
written about the politics of my native state at regular intervals for
more than three decades. After watching the Democrats’ century-long rule
in Texas come to a decisive end with Gov. Ann Richards’s loss to George W.
Bush in 1994, I saw the party descend into atrophy in which failure begot
more failure. “The 30-year drought has done a lot of things,” said Luke
Warford, the chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party and the
founder of the Agave Democratic Infrastructure Fund. “It’s kept donors on
the sidelines, which makes a lot of potentially good candidates not run
because there’s no belief they can win. And it also makes a lot of really
talented staff leave to find better-paying work in true battleground
states.” The Democratic Party has no counterpart to Mr. Abbott, and hasn’t
since 1993, when Senator Lloyd Bentsen moved to Washington to join
President Bill Clinton’s cabinet. Its weaknesses are even more glaring
farther down the hierarchy. In recent elections, as many as one-third of
state races have gone uncontested by Democrats. One-fifth of the party’s
county chairs and two-thirds of its precinct chairs have been left
unfilled. Until last year, the state party had a negative operating
budget. As the veteran Democratic consultant Matt Angle observed, “There’s
been a hollowing-out of the party.” Still, those of us who recall the
satisfied sense of invincibility among Texas Democrats after roughly a
century of one-party rule have detected similar signs of overconfidence
among the state’s ruling party. The party’s rightward tilt, increasingly
forceful with each legislative session, reached its apotheosis in March,
with Mr. Paxton’s primary victory over the more moderate Republican
four-term incumbent, Senator John Cornyn. Mr. Paxton, a close ally of Mr.
Trump’s, was impeached by the Republican-controlled State House (and later
acquitted by the State Senate) in 2023 over allegations that included
bribery. He was also accused by his wife of adultery. Mr. Trump endorsed
him anyway, all but guaranteeing his landslide primary triumph over Mr.
Cornyn but in the process testing the allegiance of center-right Texans.
In similar fashion, the Texas G.O.P. is in danger of losing many Latino
voters who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 after years of siding with
Democrats. “We adopted a lazy way of campaigning that bit us on the ass,
and we’ve learned from that,” Mr. O’Rourke said. “Now it’s the Republicans
who’ve gotten really lazy and complacent and comfortable.” Signs of
Republican Overreach Simply spending one week driving through the vastness
of Texas, as I did in September, is all it takes to appreciate an underdog
party’s uphill battle. The state’s 32 million residents are spread across
20 media markets, many of them distinct ecosystems, from the urban colossi
of Houston and the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex to the oil patch of the
Texas Panhandle to the Latino-dominated borderlands of the Rio Grande
Valley. “When national donors are deciding where to invest, they look at a
place like Iowa, where $5 million can fully fund a race,” said Katherine
Fischer, the director of the Texas Majority PAC, which was established by
the liberal philanthropist Soros family. “That’s why Texas is always at
the bottom of their list. It’s just so damned big.” Reaching so many
markets presents a daunting challenge for an upstart candidate like Ms.
Hinojosa, a state representative from the border city of Brownsville.
“There’s still 20 percent of the electorate that doesn’t know who I am,”
she said in an interview in mid-September. To date, Ms. Hinojosa’s
campaign has said that it has raised about $20 million. For his part, Mr.
Talarico spent about $30 million earlier this year to introduce himself
statewide as a man of Christian faith and a member of the Texas House with
a record of supporting bipartisan legislation. Since that time, however,
Mr. Paxton and his associates have invested more than $100 million in an
effort to redefine his opponent as “radical” and “weird,” with ads that
quote from remarks Mr. Talarico made several years ago (and later
renounced) suggesting that “God is nonbinary” and that there are six
biological sexes. Mr. Paxton and his allies have at times questioned Mr.
Talarico’s manhood and even his Christianity, an effort to jolt the
sensibilities of a state prone to mythologizing godly and masculine
archetypes. “How they’re negatively defining Talarico is kind of a
bank-shot way of saying that he’s not a true Texas conservative,” Mr.
Henson said. Whether money can overwhelm conditions on the ground is the
riddle looming over the Texas races. In the border city of Laredo, which
Mr. Trump won in 2024 — the first time a Republican had done so in over a
century — signs of buyer’s remorse are evident. Arrests by Immigration and
Customs Enforcement agents in Laredo were higher in July than in any other
American city. Mr. Trump’s erratic trade policies have further created
instability at the city’s port of entry. While acknowledging the economic
concerns that many border residents share, Adrian Zapata, a business
executive in the health industry who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, said in
an interview that the negative ads against Mr. Talarico were resonating
with some of his family members. “They see Talarico as an ultraliberal,”
he said. “They’re done with the ‘they/them.’ They’re going to vote for
Paxton just because of that.” As for Mr. Zapata, “I’m not ready to vote
for Talarico,” he said. “But I don’t like Paxton. He’s never done anything
for South Texas, and his personal and business dealings have hurt him a
lot with folks down here.” There is a similarly muddled electoral picture
in the cattle country of deep West Texas adjacent to Big Bend National
Park. Mr. Trump and Mr. Abbott have aggressively championed a border wall
and artificial intelligence data centers, both of which threaten to
disrupt the region’s pastoral ethos. A coalition of more than 200
landowners has sued the federal government over the border wall, while
other residents have circulated a petition to protest the construction of
a new data center near Fort Stockton. George Johnson, a cattle feed
operator in Alpine, waved off such concerns, saying: “Folks worrying about
data centers were also worried when the internet got started. It’s
Talarico who scares me to death, him and all that socialist talk.” Others
in this largely conservative region harbor the view that Republicans have
failed to make good on their promises. Thaddeus Cleveland, the Republican
sheriff of Terrell County, said that both he and his county had voted for
Mr. Trump in 2024, but added, “Everything he campaigned on, we’re seeing
the opposite of, like going to war.” Sheriff Cleveland predicted that the
negative campaign ads by the Republicans would not factor as significantly
into the votes of his neighbors as “the price of groceries and gas, which
are compounded here because we’re so far from everywhere else.” But it is
in purple Tarrant County, dominated by Fort Worth, where the party could
pay the price for having potentially overestimated its mandate from the
voters. Conservative leaders have cut funds for nonprofits that aid
at-risk children, subjected school library books to right-wing litmus
tests and eliminated free bus rides to polling stations in poor
neighborhoods. “The far-right leaders here have implemented Project 2025
on a county level,” said Alisa Simmons, a Democrat and county commissioner
who is running to unseat the conservative county judge, Tim O’Hare. In an
early sign this year that area Republicans may be out of step with Tarrant
County’s constituents, a Democratic aviation machinist and union leader,
Taylor Rehmet, defeated Leigh Wambsganss, a well-funded Republican
Christian activist who led the conservative takeover of several metroplex
school boards. He won by 14 points in a January special election for a
State Senate seat covering a region that Mr. Trump won by 17 points in
2024. A ‘Gradualist’ Theory Which party prevails in Texas is a complicated
riddle. Historically a low-turnout state — it ranked second to last in the
2024 election, ahead of only Arkansas — Texas held a primary in March that
saw nearly one in four voters showing up to the polls, a modern record for
midterm participation, with Democrats slightly outpacing Republicans. A
few factors could conspire to thwart a blue wave in Texas. As of 2020,
straight-ticket voting is no longer possible in the state, which could
impact the mostly Democratic urban counties where that practice has
frequently been used by voters in past elections. Texas is one of only
eight states that lack universal online registration, while voting by mail
is also highly restricted. In January, Mr. Abbott turned over the state’s
list of approximately 18.7 million registered voters to the Trump
administration, and 1.2 million of them have subsequently been put on the
“suspense list” because their addresses have not been verified. The recent
shuttering of nearly one-third of Tarrant County’s polling sites by its
Republican-controlled county commission is particularly worrisome for
Democrats. “The reason we’ve lost these statewide races in the past is
because we’ve never gotten enough out of Tarrant County to overcome the
margins in rural Texas,” Ms. Davis said of the turnout. “If we don’t get
it to 53 or 54 percent this November, it’s game over. James and Gina can’t
win.” But the state’s Republicans have reasons of their own to be fretful.
Partly because of the recruitment efforts of the Texas Majority PAC and
Blueprint Texas, a down-ballot candidate support organization co-founded
by Ms. Davis earlier this year, the Democrats are fielding a full slate in
all 150 state races for the first time in a half-century. Though many of
these aspirants face long odds, their presence on the ballot could
energize the Democrats in predominantly conservative regions who have not
bothered to turn out in the past. “If we win on Nov. 3, most of those
names running down-ballot in really tough areas like East Texas and the
Hill Country and the Panhandle will be responsible,” Mr. O’Rourke said.
Mr. Henson added that while he remained skeptical about Democratic
enthusiasm being sufficient to carry the day for Mr. Talarico, he also
doubted that a last-minute avalanche of negative ads would prove decisive
for Mr. Paxton. “At a certain point, there’s diminishing impact once you
get past an absurd level of spending,” he said. Rather than project a
winner in November, Mr. Henson said he felt more comfortable embracing a
“gradualist” theory, one in which Texas does not become blue overnight,
but instead competitive. “Even if Talarico loses by a Beto-like margin,”
he said, “the next cycle is a presidential election, where Trump likely
won’t be popular and Democratic turnout will be higher. So there are

[ ]CONTRIBUTE Thank you, James Talarico [ ]'New York Times: In Texas, Talarico Inspires a Recurring Blue-Tinted Dream In the go-big-or-go-home collective consciousness of Texas, no ambition is deemed too reckless, no daydream too wild. Save perhaps one. It is the idea, fantastical to many as it is irresistible to others, that the Democrats will win a statewide race in Texas for the first time in 32 years. According to the latest New York Times/Siena University poll of the race for U.S. Senate, James Talarico, a 37-year-old state legislator seen by national Democrats as one of the breakout stars of this cycle, is ahead of his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, the state’s scandal-plagued attorney general, by six points. The poll was conducted from Sept. 21 to Sept. 30. A survey from mid-September, the ReconMR/Siena Research Institute poll, also showed the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Gina Hinojosa, four points ahead of the three-term G.O.P. incumbent, Greg Abbott, the most dominant political figure in Texas. Cue the fluttering heartbeats. Cue, as well, the eye-rolls. Given how thoroughly Republicans have dominated the state, and how the hopes of Democrats have repeatedly crashed, some Texas pollsters remain skeptical. “At some point, you do get conditioned by all that’s happened in the past,” said James Henson, the director of the University of Texas at Austin’s Texas Politics Project. “I mean, you look at the trends and you have to admit that something’s going on. But you still don’t want to believe your lying eyes, because you’ve been burned for so long.” Mr. Henson was referring to the perennial spectacle of much-ballyhooed Texas Democratic aspirants face-planting against the Lone Star State’s red wall. First came Tony Sanchez Jr., the swaggering and self-funding Laredo oilman whom Gov. Rick Perry dispatched in 2002 by an 18-point margin. Next was the state senator Wendy Davis, who attracted worldwide attention for her filibuster in the Texas Legislature against an anti-abortion measure but whom Mr. Abbott demolished by 20 points in 2014. Finally, the El Paso congressman Beto O’Rourke came up 2.6 points short of defeating Senator Ted Cruz in 2018 but then suffered a 10-point loss to Mr. Abbott four years later. Even with the awareness of such humiliations, Democrats find themselves maintaining that 2026 could, at long last, be the year. President Trump’s deep unpopularity and the prospect of a blue wave could, they insist, extend into the state he won by nearly 14 points in 2024. According to a September survey conducted by Texas Southern University, Mr. Trump is seven points underwater in Texas. Mr. Talarico has run an energetic and well-financed campaign, while Mr. Paxton has staged far fewer public events and has had to rely on outside groups to fund an attack-ad blitzkrieg against his Democratic opponent. Mr. Abbott, meanwhile, has outspent Ms. Hinojosa by a 10-to-one ratio, yet has been unable to build an insurmountable lead. “People have vastly underestimated Gina,” said Ms. Davis, now a political consultant and a senior adviser to Planned Parenthood Texas Votes, an advocacy organization. “Dollar for dollar, she’s running the best statewide campaign we’ve ever seen.” Such optimism stands in defiance of the political axiom that Texas is where idealistic Democrats go to be mugged by reality. The party’s demise there is not a product of ill fortune, Mr. Henson said. “Governor Abbott has built an impressive election machine that has benefited state-level Republicans again and again for a decade and a half,” he said. “And the Democratic machinery here is almost nonexistent.” A ‘Hollowing-Out’ I have written about the politics of my native state at regular intervals for more than three decades. After watching the Democrats’ century-long rule in Texas come to a decisive end with Gov. Ann Richards’s loss to George W. Bush in 1994, I saw the party descend into atrophy in which failure begot more failure. “The 30-year drought has done a lot of things,” said Luke Warford, the chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party and the founder of the Agave Democratic Infrastructure Fund. “It’s kept donors on the sidelines, which makes a lot of potentially good candidates not run because there’s no belief they can win. And it also makes a lot of really talented staff leave to find better-paying work in true battleground states.” The Democratic Party has no counterpart to Mr. Abbott, and hasn’t since 1993, when Senator Lloyd Bentsen moved to Washington to join President Bill Clinton’s cabinet. Its weaknesses are even more glaring farther down the hierarchy. In recent elections, as many as one-third of state races have gone uncontested by Democrats. One-fifth of the party’s county chairs and two-thirds of its precinct chairs have been left unfilled. Until last year, the state party had a negative operating budget. As the veteran Democratic consultant Matt Angle observed, “There’s been a hollowing-out of the party.” Still, those of us who recall the satisfied sense of invincibility among Texas Democrats after roughly a century of one-party rule have detected similar signs of overconfidence among the state’s ruling party. The party’s rightward tilt, increasingly forceful with each legislative session, reached its apotheosis in March, with Mr. Paxton’s primary victory over the more moderate Republican four-term incumbent, Senator John Cornyn. Mr. Paxton, a close ally of Mr. Trump’s, was impeached by the Republican-controlled State House (and later acquitted by the State Senate) in 2023 over allegations that included bribery. He was also accused by his wife of adultery. Mr. Trump endorsed him anyway, all but guaranteeing his landslide primary triumph over Mr. Cornyn but in the process testing the allegiance of center-right Texans. In similar fashion, the Texas G.O.P. is in danger of losing many Latino voters who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 after years of siding with Democrats. “We adopted a lazy way of campaigning that bit us on the ass, and we’ve learned from that,” Mr. O’Rourke said. “Now it’s the Republicans who’ve gotten really lazy and complacent and comfortable.” Signs of Republican Overreach Simply spending one week driving through the vastness of Texas, as I did in September, is all it takes to appreciate an underdog party’s uphill battle. The state’s 32 million residents are spread across 20 media markets, many of them distinct ecosystems, from the urban colossi of Houston and the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex to the oil patch of the Texas Panhandle to the Latino-dominated borderlands of the Rio Grande Valley. “When national donors are deciding where to invest, they look at a place like Iowa, where $5 million can fully fund a race,” said Katherine Fischer, the director of the Texas Majority PAC, which was established by the liberal philanthropist Soros family. “That’s why Texas is always at the bottom of their list. It’s just so damned big.” Reaching so many markets presents a daunting challenge for an upstart candidate like Ms. Hinojosa, a state representative from the border city of Brownsville. “There’s still 20 percent of the electorate that doesn’t know who I am,” she said in an interview in mid-September. To date, Ms. Hinojosa’s campaign has said that it has raised about $20 million. For his part, Mr. Talarico spent about $30 million earlier this year to introduce himself statewide as a man of Christian faith and a member of the Texas House with a record of supporting bipartisan legislation. Since that time, however, Mr. Paxton and his associates have invested more than $100 million in an effort to redefine his opponent as “radical” and “weird,” with ads that quote from remarks Mr. Talarico made several years ago (and later renounced) suggesting that “God is nonbinary” and that there are six biological sexes. Mr. Paxton and his allies have at times questioned Mr. Talarico’s manhood and even his Christianity, an effort to jolt the sensibilities of a state prone to mythologizing godly and masculine archetypes. “How they’re negatively defining Talarico is kind of a bank-shot way of saying that he’s not a true Texas conservative,” Mr. Henson said. Whether money can overwhelm conditions on the ground is the riddle looming over the Texas races. In the border city of Laredo, which Mr. Trump won in 2024 — the first time a Republican had done so in over a century — signs of buyer’s remorse are evident. Arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Laredo were higher in July than in any other American city. Mr. Trump’s erratic trade policies have further created instability at the city’s port of entry. While acknowledging the economic concerns that many border residents share, Adrian Zapata, a business executive in the health industry who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, said in an interview that the negative ads against Mr. Talarico were resonating with some of his family members. “They see Talarico as an ultraliberal,” he said. “They’re done with the ‘they/them.’ They’re going to vote for Paxton just because of that.” As for Mr. Zapata, “I’m not ready to vote for Talarico,” he said. “But I don’t like Paxton. He’s never done anything for South Texas, and his personal and business dealings have hurt him a lot with folks down here.” There is a similarly muddled electoral picture in the cattle country of deep West Texas adjacent to Big Bend National Park. Mr. Trump and Mr. Abbott have aggressively championed a border wall and artificial intelligence data centers, both of which threaten to disrupt the region’s pastoral ethos. A coalition of more than 200 landowners has sued the federal government over the border wall, while other residents have circulated a petition to protest the construction of a new data center near Fort Stockton. George Johnson, a cattle feed operator in Alpine, waved off such concerns, saying: “Folks worrying about data centers were also worried when the internet got started. It’s Talarico who scares me to death, him and all that socialist talk.” Others in this largely conservative region harbor the view that Republicans have failed to make good on their promises. Thaddeus Cleveland, the Republican sheriff of Terrell County, said that both he and his county had voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, but added, “Everything he campaigned on, we’re seeing the opposite of, like going to war.” Sheriff Cleveland predicted that the negative campaign ads by the Republicans would not factor as significantly into the votes of his neighbors as “the price of groceries and gas, which are compounded here because we’re so far from everywhere else.” But it is in purple Tarrant County, dominated by Fort Worth, where the party could pay the price for having potentially overestimated its mandate from the voters. Conservative leaders have cut funds for nonprofits that aid at-risk children, subjected school library books to right-wing litmus tests and eliminated free bus rides to polling stations in poor neighborhoods. “The far-right leaders here have implemented Project 2025 on a county level,” said Alisa Simmons, a Democrat and county commissioner who is running to unseat the conservative county judge, Tim O’Hare. In an early sign this year that area Republicans may be out of step with Tarrant County’s constituents, a Democratic aviation machinist and union leader, Taylor Rehmet, defeated Leigh Wambsganss, a well-funded Republican Christian activist who led the conservative takeover of several metroplex school boards. He won by 14 points in a January special election for a State Senate seat covering a region that Mr. Trump won by 17 points in 2024. A ‘Gradualist’ Theory Which party prevails in Texas is a complicated riddle. Historically a low-turnout state — it ranked second to last in the 2024 election, ahead of only Arkansas — Texas held a primary in March that saw nearly one in four voters showing up to the polls, a modern record for midterm participation, with Democrats slightly outpacing Republicans. A few factors could conspire to thwart a blue wave in Texas. As of 2020, straight-ticket voting is no longer possible in the state, which could impact the mostly Democratic urban counties where that practice has frequently been used by voters in past elections. Texas is one of only eight states that lack universal online registration, while voting by mail is also highly restricted. In January, Mr. Abbott turned over the state’s list of approximately 18.7 million registered voters to the Trump administration, and 1.2 million of them have subsequently been put on the “suspense list” because their addresses have not been verified. The recent shuttering of nearly one-third of Tarrant County’s polling sites by its Republican-controlled county commission is particularly worrisome for Democrats. “The reason we’ve lost these statewide races in the past is because we’ve never gotten enough out of Tarrant County to overcome the margins in rural Texas,” Ms. Davis said of the turnout. “If we don’t get it to 53 or 54 percent this November, it’s game over. James and Gina can’t win.” But the state’s Republicans have reasons of their own to be fretful. Partly because of the recruitment efforts of the Texas Majority PAC and Blueprint Texas, a down-ballot candidate support organization co-founded by Ms. Davis earlier this year, the Democrats are fielding a full slate in all 150 state races for the first time in a half-century. Though many of these aspirants face long odds, their presence on the ballot could energize the Democrats in predominantly conservative regions who have not bothered to turn out in the past. “If we win on Nov. 3, most of those names running down-ballot in really tough areas like East Texas and the Hill Country and the Panhandle will be responsible,” Mr. O’Rourke said. Mr. Henson added that while he remained skeptical about Democratic enthusiasm being sufficient to carry the day for Mr. Talarico, he also doubted that a last-minute avalanche of negative ads would prove decisive for Mr. Paxton. “At a certain point, there’s diminishing impact once you get past an absurd level of spending,” he said. Rather than project a winner in November, Mr. Henson said he felt more comfortable embracing a “gradualist” theory, one in which Texas does not become blue overnight, but instead competitive. “Even if Talarico loses by a Beto-like margin,” he said, “the next cycle is a presidential election, where Trump likely won’t be popular and Democratic turnout will be higher. clean_body: No tricks. Just a midnight deadline. No tricks. Just a midnight deadline. | Peter, Last Halloween, I had only just gotten home from a deployment to Iraq. I remember thinking how good it was to be back in a country where the scariest thing on the street was a kid in a plastic mask. A year later, I'm running for Congress. And I've learned that some of the scariest things in this race pretend to be things they are not. Christina Hines pretends to be a prosecutor. Pull off the mask, and her record tells a different story. Fifteen felony charges, dismissed in a single hearing, with Hines in the courtroom. A case involving a 12-year-old victim assaulted, that ended in just probation for the criminal. Case, after case, Soro's backed results. And standing right behind her? Hakeem Jeffries, waiting for the Speaker's gavel. If Democrats flip seats like MI-10, that's not a bad dream. That's January. So here 's the trick: there isn't one. Tonight at midnight is the final end-of-month deadline of this campaign. When the clock strikes twelve, it's over. No extensions. No second chances. We 're still $5,786 short of our goal. Will you treat this campaign to $10, $25, or whatever you can before midnight? | Thank you, and stay safe out there tonight. For God and Country, Mike Bouchard Army Paratrooper | Bronze Star Recipient | Paid for by Friends of Michael Bouchard, Inc. Michael Bouchard is a member of the Army National Guard. Live on Red Bull, coffee, and sheer will.| | | Friend, nice to meet you, _I’m Joy._ I am one of the tactical operatives here at Voters for Tomorrow Action Fund, and I specialize in keeping our down-ballot legislative campaigns alive.If you want to know what the final 48 hours before Election Day actually look like for the people running your defense lines, let me give it to you straight:
---
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/142639703/657559034/-960263130?refcode=joysask251031text&sourceid=1142367&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNjEvMS8xMTE3NzMiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiZWJiNmY1MDAtODNkNS1mMTExLWJmNWItMDAwZDNhNTQ0NDJlIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=sVwv54bPN66ch4tqQtWn13sioj4pJ1F3xD_XiID193Y=)
---
_We are working 20-hour days, living entirely off Red Bull, lukewarm coffee, and the high-stakes adrenaline of a campaign that cannot afford to fail._**Right now, the headlines are celebrating that 52 million Americans have already voted.** That is an incredible achievement that all of us played a part in to make happen this year. _**But there are 234 million eligible voters in this country,** which means the margins that will decide this election are still sitting on their couches._We are doing the grueling, unglamorous work of dragging, convincing, and reengaging to get those voters to the polls. **Our down-ballot candidates are the true boots on the ground.** They are carrying the literature for the top of the ticket on their backs, knocking on doors in the toughest districts to ensure we have the legislative firewall necessary to stop extremist redistricting efforts.But these bootstrapped campaigns are being massively outspent, and our 24/7 candidate hotline is ringing off the hook. Their biggest panic right now? _**Voter protection.**_ The opposition is mobilizing to deploy federal "observers" into heavy Democratic precincts to intimidate our communities. Our candidates need advanced data, tight scripts, and immediate legal resources on Tuesday to ensure every single vote is cast, counted, and protected.[You already know about the massive matching challenge our donor put up. Thanks to you, we have raised exactly half of it.](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/142639704/657559035/-960263130?refcode=joysask251031text&sourceid=1142367&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNjEvMS8xMTE3NzMiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiZWJiNmY1MDAtODNkNS1mMTExLWJmNWItMDAwZDNhNTQ0NDJlIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=sVwv54bPN66ch4tqQtWn13sioj4pJ1F3xD_XiID193Y=) **I am reaching out from the war room because we need to close the remaining gap in the next 48 hours.** We have stretched every single dollar, but we cannot fully deploy our Election Protection Operation on Tuesday if we do not hit this goal today.**We are supplying the grit. We need you to supply the fuel.**

That is an incredible achievement that all of us played a part in to make happen this year. But there are 234 million eligible voters in this country, which means the margins that will decide this election are still sitting on their couches.We are doing the grueling, unglamorous work of dragging, convincing, and reengaging to get those voters to the polls. Our down-ballot candidates are the true boots on the ground. Their biggest panic right now? Voter protection. The opposition is mobilizing to deploy federal "observers" into heavy Democratic precincts to intimidate our communities. Our candidates need advanced data, tight scripts, and immediate legal resources on Tuesday to ensure every single vote is cast, counted, and protected.= I am reaching out from the war room because we need to close the remaining gap in the next 48 hours. clean_body: I've seen firsthand what's at stake in these final days. | = Peter, Over the last few weeks, I've traveled from Ohio to New Jersey, Georgia, and Virginia — knocking doors alongside volunteers, meeting with candidates, and talking with voters about the issues that matter most to their communities. After everything I've seen on the ground, one thing is clear:These races are going to be close. Election Day is just three days away. And what happens in these final 72 hours could determine whether all of the work we've put in this cycle — the recruiting, organizing, training, and investments we've made in our campaigns — is enough to take back power at every level of government. = | = In a close race, the final result can come down to who works harder, who reaches more voters, and who leaves nothing on the table. I've seen that determination firsthand in our candidates and their teams. But I also know that they need the resources to keep fighting until the very last polls close. Because there's a difference between a winnable race and actually winning. Women like Dr. Amy Acton in Ohio , Rebecca Bennett in New Jersey , Tanya Miller in Georgia , and dozens more EMILYs List candidates are competing in critical races where every last vote matters. Listen, I know you're tired of these messages. Me too.

Every campaign is fighting for your attention and your hard-earned cash. Some will even take your $5, then do _absolutely nothing with it._

So let me tell you why your $5 will go ten times further in our fight to defeat Susan Collins and flip the Senate. Then, I'm going to ask you please, **[please invest in our campaign in the final 3 days of this election.](https://substack.com/redirect/940aa3aa-8250-4168-8e37-2fae9a956189?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
[ CHIP IN NOW ->](https://substack.com/redirect/940aa3aa-8250-4168-8e37-2fae9a956189?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
**FACT:** Every dollar we raise gets invested into my campaign immediately. TV ads, voter turnout efforts, supplies for our office, yard signs -- you name it.

**FACT: Susan Collins and her cronies have spent $114 million to defeat me.** This will fund their brutal attack ads and on-the-ground operations to reach Maine's 6% of undecided voters.

**FACT:** A new poll just came out showing me **losing to Susan Collins by 0.5%.** No, that's not a typo. This is the closest Senate race in the country.

**FACT:** If we don't raise at least $13,000 from this very email, we will miss our end-of-month fundraising goal. That's not an exaggeration.

This late in the game, if we miss a fundraising goal, it doesn't come out in the wash. In fact, it snowballs into a bigger issue. And suddenly, we need to take down our TV ads early. _We cannot do that if we want to win._

**[I'm down by half a point in the last 3 days, and EVERY dollar matters in this fight to defeat Susan Collins and flip the Senate. I really don't want to let people down if we come up short, so will you please give $5 or more before our midnight fundraising deadline?](https://substack.com/redirect/940aa3aa-8250-4168-8e37-2fae9a956189?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
[CHIP IN NOW ->](https://substack.com/redirect/940aa3aa-8250-4168-8e37-2fae9a956189?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Please -- I really hope you'll pull through for me.

Solidarity forever,
Troy
